newsitem.title: INDIA: Strike hits Bombay as workers mourn slain leader.
newsitem.headline: Strike hits Bombay as workers mourn slain leader.

text.p: Security was tightened in India's commercial capital on Friday after trade unions called a general strike to protest the killing of prominent trade unionist Datta Samant, police said.
Datta Samant, 65, was shot dead in a Bombay suburb by four unidentified gunmen on Thursday.
The strike call coincided with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's visit to Bombay, prompting police to bring in reinforcements from surrounding areas.
The mafia-style killing sent shock waves through India's labour movement, and union leaders said they would organise demonstrations to protest Samant's death.
Police said they suspected inter-union rivalry as the motive for the killing. Businessmen say organised crime has infiltrated trade unions in the city of 13 million people.
Deve Gowda is due to meet Reserve Bank of India governor Chakravarty Rangarajan in a courtesy call during his visit.

In Bombay's central and eastern suburbs, where textile mills employing members of Samant's trade unions are concentrated, life was virtually paralysed with shops closed, and buses and taxis off the streets.
In other areas, shops were open although fewer buses and taxis ran. Train services were normal.
A few isolated stone-throwing incidents were reported in some suburbs on Thursday, but no serious violence occurred, said state deputy chief minister Gopinath Munde.
But police said expected protests by various trade unions and Samant's funeral, scheduled to begin around 10 a.m. (0430 GMT), could spark some incidents.
"We are not taking any chances," one police source said.
Police said Samant and his son were travelling in a jeep when the attackers opened fire from a motor-rickshaw in the central suburb of Powai.
Samant's chauffeur was seriously wounded, but the union leader's son escaped unhurt.
A doctor who gave up his profession for militant trade unionism, Samant shot into the spotlight in the early 1980s when he led a two-year-long strike by textile workers in Bombay.
He later became a member of the Maharashtra state legislature and was elected to the national parliament.
Samant was also a critic of India's mafia-style gangs.
Trade unionists and politicians, many of whom are expected to join the funeral procession, condemned the killing.
